text:
Parajikapali - First Parajika

17. Or further, if a <term>samaneru</term> <gloss>novice monk</gloss> is restless, dissatisfied, or wishing to abandon the training; being humiliated, ashamed, disgusted, desiring the householder life—up to—desiring the state of one who is not a son of the Sakyans, he says, "I have a mother, she will provide for me," and speaks distractedly; he says, "I have a father, he will provide for me," and speaks distractedly; he says, "I have a brother, he will provide for me," and speaks distractedly; he says, "I have a sister, she will provide for me," and speaks distractedly; he says, "I have a son, he will provide for me," and speaks distractedly; he says, "I have a daughter, she will provide for me," and speaks distractedly; he says, "I have a wife, she will provide for me," and speaks distractedly; he says, "I have relatives, they will provide for me," and speaks distractedly; he says, "I have friends, they will provide for me," and speaks distractedly; he says, "I have a village, from which I will live," and speaks distractedly; he says, "I have a town, from which I will live," and speaks distractedly; he says, "I have a field, from which I will live," and speaks distractedly; he says, "I have an estate, from which I will live," and speaks distractedly; he says, "I have money, from which I will live," and speaks distractedly; he says, "I have gold, from which I will live," and speaks distractedly—up to—he says, "I have a craft, from which I will live," and speaks distractedly. Even in this way, monks, the weakness is expressed and the training is renounced.

18. Or further, if a <term>samaneru</term> <gloss>novice monk</gloss> is restless, dissatisfied, or wishing to abandon the training; being humiliated, ashamed, disgusted, desiring the householder life—up to—desiring the state of one who is not a son of the Sakyans, he says, "It is difficult," and speaks distractedly; he says, "It is troublesome," and speaks distractedly; he says, "It is burdensome," and speaks distractedly; he says, "It is not easy," and speaks distractedly; he says, "I am not able," and speaks distractedly; he says, "I cannot trust myself," and speaks distractedly; he says, "I do not find joy," and speaks distractedly—up to—he says, "I do not find satisfaction," and speaks distractedly. Even in this way, monks, the weakness is expressed and the training is renounced.

19. And how, monks, is the weakness expressed and the training renounced? Here, monks, a <term>bhikkhu</term> <gloss>ordained monk</gloss> or a <term>samaneru</term> <gloss>novice monk</gloss> who is restless, dissatisfied, or wishing to abandon the training; being humiliated, ashamed, disgusted, desiring the householder life—up to—desiring the state of one who is not a son of the Sakyans, he says, "I renounce the Buddha," and speaks distractedly. Even in this way, monks, the weakness is expressed and the training is renounced.

<summary>This passage continues the technical definition of how a novice or monk expresses dissatisfaction with the monastic life, detailing various ways in which one might declare their intent to leave the order through claims of family obligations, financial concerns, or lack of personal ability.</summary>
